title: Domain-specific architecture
text:
One of the application domains where DSA have found the most success is that of artificial intelligence. In particular, several architectures have been developed for the acceleration of Deep Neural Networks (DNN).[1] In the following sections, we report some examples.

### TPU

Google's TPU was developed in 2015 to accelerate DNN inference since the company projected that the use of voice search would require to double the computational resources allocated at the time for neural network inference.[2]

The TPU was designed to be a co-processor communicating via a PCIe bus, to be easily incorporated in existing servers. It is primarily a matrix-multiplication engine following a CISC (Complex Instruction Set Computer) ISA. The multiplication engine uses systolic execution to save energy, reducing the number of writes to SRAM.[3]

The TPU was fabricated with a 28-nm process and clocked at 700 MHz. The portion of the application that runs on the TPU is implemented in TensorFlow.[3]

The TPU computes primarily reduced precision integers, which further contributes to energy savings and increased performance.[3]

### Microsoft Catapult

Microsoft's Project Catapult[4] put an FPGA connected through a PCIe bus into data center servers, with the idea of using the FPGA to accelerate various applications running on the server, leveraging the reconfiguration capabilities of FPGA to accelerate many different applications.

Differently from Google's TPU, the Catapult FPGA needed to be programmed via hardware-description languages such as Verilog and VHDL. For this reason, a major concern for the authors of the framework was the limited programmability.[5]

Microsoft designed a CNN accelerator for the Catapult framework that was primarily designed to accelerate the ranking function in the Bing search engine. The proposed architecture provided a runtime reconfigurable design based on a two-dimensional systolic array.[6,7]

### NVDLA

NVDLA is NVIDIA's deep-learning inference accelerator. It is an open-source hardware design available in a number of highly parametrizable configurations. The small-NVDLA model is designed to be deployed in resource-constrained scenarios such as IoT where cost, area and power are the main concerns. Conversely. the large-NVDLA model is more suitable for HPC scenarios. NVDLA provides its own dedicated training infrastructure, compilation tools and runtime software stack.[8]
